claim: A fundamental aspect of human experience is that it is segmented into discrete events.
source: A fundamental aspect of human experience is that it is segmented into discrete events.
evidence: This is a general statement about human experience that draws from established understanding in cognitive science.

claim: Event segmentation may be underpinned by transitions between distinct neural states.
source: This may be underpinned by transitions between distinct neural states.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the neural basis of event segmentation.

claim: Neural state boundaries are organized in a temporal cortical hierarchy, with short states in primary sensory regions, and long states in lateral and medial prefrontal cortex.
source: Our results show that neural state boundaries are organized in a temporal cortical hierarchy, with short states in primary sensory regions, and long states in lateral and medial prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the study, as shown in Figure 1.

claim: State boundaries are shared within and between groups of brain regions that resemble well-known functional networks.
source: State boundaries are shared within and between groups of brain regions that resemble well-known functional networks.
evidence: This is supported by the connectivity analyses and network identification presented in the study, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Perceived event boundaries overlap with neural state boundaries across large parts of the cortical hierarchy.
source: Perceived event boundaries overlap with neural state boundaries across large parts of the cortical hierarchy, particularly when those state boundaries demarcate a strong transition or are shared between brain regions.
evidence: This is supported by the overlap analyses presented in the study, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: Perceived event boundaries particularly overlap with neural state boundaries when those state boundaries demarcate a strong transition.
source: Perceived event boundaries overlap with neural state boundaries across large parts of the cortical hierarchy, particularly when those state boundaries demarcate a strong transition or are shared between brain regions.
evidence: This is supported by the boundary strength analysis presented in the study, as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Perceived event boundaries particularly overlap with neural state boundaries when those boundaries are shared between brain regions.
source: Perceived event boundaries overlap with neural state boundaries across large parts of the cortical hierarchy, particularly when those state boundaries demarcate a strong transition or are shared between brain regions.
evidence: This is supported by the co-occurrence analyses presented in the study, as shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: A partially nested cortical hierarchy of neural states forms the basis of event segmentation.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that a partially nested cortical hierarchy of neural states forms the basis of event segmentation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined results of the study.

claim: Spatial information processing is characterized by segmenting spatial regions into objects.
source: Spatial information processing is characterized by segmenting spatial regions into objects (e.g., DiCarlo and Cox, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Temporal information processing is characterized by segmenting our ongoing experience into separate events.
source: In a similar way, temporal information processing is characterized by segmenting our ongoing experience into separate events (Kurby and Zacks, 2008; Newtson et al., 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Segmentation improves our understanding of ongoing perceptual input.
source: Segmentation improves our understanding of ongoing perceptual input (Zacks et al., 2001a) and allows us to recall distinct events from our past (Flores et al., 2017; Sargent et al., 2013; Zacks et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Segmentation allows us to recall distinct events from our past.
source: Segmentation improves our understanding of ongoing perceptual input (Zacks et al., 2001a) and allows us to recall distinct events from our past (Flores et al., 2017; Sargent et al., 2013; Zacks et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The end of an event triggers an evoked response in the hippocampus.
source: Recent work has shown that the end of an event triggers an evoked response in the hippocampus (Baldassano et al., 2017; Ben-Yakov and Henson, 2018), suggesting that events form the basis of long-term memory representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Events form the basis of long-term memory representations.
source: Recent work has shown that the end of an event triggers an evoked response in the hippocampus (Baldassano et al., 2017; Ben-Yakov and Henson, 2018), suggesting that events form the basis of long-term memory representations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited work about hippocampal responses.

claim: Events that are identified in written, auditory, and audiovisual narratives (movies) are often very similar across individuals.
source: Events that are identified in written, auditory, and audiovisual narratives (movies) are often very similar across individuals and can be segmented hierarchically on different timescales (Newtson and Rindner, 1979; Zacks et al., 2001a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Events can be segmented hierarchically on different timescales.
source: Events that are identified in written, auditory, and audiovisual narratives (movies) are often very similar across individuals and can be segmented hierarchically on different timescales (Newtson and Rindner, 1979; Zacks et al., 2001a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: According to event segmentation theory (EST), perceptual systems spontaneously segment activity into meaningful events as a side effect of predicting future information.
source: According to event segmentation theory (EST), perceptual systems spontaneously segment activity into meaningful events as a side effect of predicting future information (Zacks et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim describes a theory from prior work.

claim: Event boundaries are perceived when predictions become less accurate.
source: That is, event boundaries are perceived when predictions become less accurate, which can be due to a change in motion or features of the situation such as characters, causes, goals, and spatial location (Zacks et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Event boundaries are observed even when a change is predictable.
source: However, event boundaries are observed even when a change is predictable, suggesting that other mechanisms play a role (Pettijohn and Radvansky, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Experiences are grouped into categories (or event types), which we have learned previously.
source: One proposal is that experiences are grouped into categories (or event types), which we have learned previously. When a new event type is detected, an event boundary occurs (Shin and DuBrow, 2021).
evidence: This claim describes a proposal from prior work.

claim: When a new event type is detected, an event boundary occurs.
source: One proposal is that experiences are grouped into categories (or event types), which we have learned previously. When a new event type is detected, an event boundary occurs (Shin and DuBrow, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Commonly identified regions showing evoked responses around event boundaries include the precuneus and medial visual cortex, as well as area V5 and the intraparietal sulcus.
source: Although the exact regions vary across studies, commonly identified regions include the precuneus and medial visual cortex, as well as area V5 and the intraparietal sulcus (Kurby and Zacks, 2018; Speer et al., 2007; Zacks et al., 2001b; Zacks et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Increased brain responses at event boundaries in these regions likely reflect updating processes that occur when shifting to a new event model.
source: Increased brain responses at event boundaries in these regions likely reflect updating processes that occur when shifting to a new event model (Ezzyat and Davachi, 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Baldassano et al., 2017 applied a data-driven method based on hidden Markov models (HMMs) to fMRI data obtained during movie watching to identify timepoints where brain activity transitioned from one temporarily stable activity pattern to a different pattern.
source: Recently, a different approach has been introduced to investigate the neural underpinnings of event segmentation (Baldassano et al., 2017). These authors applied a data-driven method, based on hidden Markov models (HMMs) to functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data obtained during movie watching to identify timepoints where brain activity in a particular region transitioned from one temporarily stable activity pattern to a different pattern.
evidence: This claim describes a method from prior work.

claim: Neural states occur on different timescales across the cortical hierarchy, with short-lived states in early sensory regions and long-lasting states in higher-level regions such as the precuneus and angular gyrus.
source: These neural states occur on different timescales across the cortical hierarchy, with short-lived states in early sensory regions and long-lasting states in higher-level regions such as the precuneus and angular gyrus (Baldassano et al., 2017), in line with previous observations of a temporal hierarchy of information processing in the brain (Hasson et al., 2008; Honey et al., 2012; Lerner et al., 2011; Stephens et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There is a temporal hierarchy of information processing in the brain.
source: These neural states occur on different timescales across the cortical hierarchy, with short-lived states in early sensory regions and long-lasting states in higher-level regions such as the precuneus and angular gyrus (Baldassano et al., 2017), in line with previous observations of a temporal hierarchy of information processing in the brain (Hasson et al., 2008; Honey et al., 2012; Lerner et al., 2011; Stephens et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: For a set of four brain regions, Baldassano et al., 2017 showed that neural state boundaries overlapped across different regions and with subjectively experienced event boundaries.
source: Interestingly, for a set of four brain regions, Baldassano et al., 2017 showed that neural state boundaries overlapped across different regions and with subjectively experienced event boundaries.
evidence: This claim describes findings from prior work.

claim: Neural state segmentation could be the source of perceived event boundaries.
source: These results suggest that neural state segmentation could be the source of perceived event boundaries and that states may be organized in a nested cortical hierarchy, such that the boundaries of faster states in regions lower in the cortical hierarchy are nested within the boundaries of slower regions higher up in the hierarchy.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of prior findings.

claim: States may be organized in a nested cortical hierarchy, such that the boundaries of faster states in regions lower in the cortical hierarchy are nested within the boundaries of slower regions higher up in the hierarchy.
source: These results suggest that neural state segmentation could be the source of perceived event boundaries and that states may be organized in a nested cortical hierarchy, such that the boundaries of faster states in regions lower in the cortical hierarchy are nested within the boundaries of slower regions higher up in the hierarchy.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the organization of neural states.

claim: In a nested hierarchy, each brain region integrates information within discretized neural states that may align with sensory units in the external environment.
source: In such a nested hierarchy, each brain region integrates information within discretized neural states that may align with sensory units in the external environment (e.g., phonemes, words, sentences) and provide its output to the brain regions higher in the cortical hierarchy (Nelson et al., 2017), until neural states at the highest level of the hierarchy align with subjectively experienced events.
evidence: This is a theoretical description supported by a citation.

claim: Information traveling up the hierarchy is gradually integrated into complex and long-lasting multimodal representations.
source: This way information traveling up the hierarchy is gradually integrated into complex and long-lasting multimodal representations (Hasson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The evidence for a nested cortical hierarchy is limited, as it has only been investigated in one previous study using four predefined regions of interest.
source: Although this is an intriguing hypothesis, the evidence for it is limited, as it has only been investigated in one previous study using four predefined regions of interest (Baldassano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature supported by a citation.

claim: It remains unknown which brain regions show neural state boundaries that align with perceived event boundaries.
source: In addition, it remains unknown which brain regions show neural state boundaries that align with perceived event boundaries and the temporal hierarchy of state segmentation remains unexplored across large parts of the cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in the literature.

claim: The temporal hierarchy of state segmentation remains unexplored across large parts of the cortex.
source: In addition, it remains unknown which brain regions show neural state boundaries that align with perceived event boundaries and the temporal hierarchy of state segmentation remains unexplored across large parts of the cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about gaps in the literature.

claim: If the brain segments ongoing input in a nested hierarchical fashion, we would expect to find especially long-lasting neural states in the frontal cortex.
source: If the brain segments ongoing input in a nested hierarchical fashion, we would expect to find especially long-lasting neural states in the frontal cortex, which is often considered the top of the cortical hierarchy (Fuster, 2001).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on established knowledge about cortical hierarchy.

claim: The frontal cortex is often considered the top of the cortical hierarchy.
source: If the brain segments ongoing input in a nested hierarchical fashion, we would expect to find especially long-lasting neural states in the frontal cortex, which is often considered the top of the cortical hierarchy (Fuster, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: We would expect to find overlap between neural state boundaries and event boundaries across all levels of the cortical hierarchy.
source: We would also expect to find overlap between neural state boundaries and event boundaries across all levels of the cortical hierarchy, although this overlap should be most consistent for areas at higher levels of the hierarchy where the timescales of neural state segmentation should closely match the experienced timescale of events.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about expected findings.

claim: Overlap between neural state boundaries and event boundaries should be most consistent for areas at higher levels of the hierarchy where the timescales of neural state segmentation should closely match the experienced timescale of events.
source: We would also expect to find overlap between neural state boundaries and event boundaries across all levels of the cortical hierarchy, although this overlap should be most consistent for areas at higher levels of the hierarchy where the timescales of neural state segmentation should closely match the experienced timescale of events.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about expected findings.

claim: State boundaries are most strongly shared between groups of brain regions involved in similar cognitive functions (i.e., networks).
source: Finally, we would expect that state boundaries are most strongly shared between groups of brain regions involved in similar cognitive functions (i.e., networks) and to a lesser extent between more distinct sets of brain areas.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about expected findings.

claim: The Cam-CAN movie dataset shows reliable stimulus-driven activity (i.e., significant inter-subject correlations) over nearly all cortical brain regions.
source: By using a large movie fMRI dataset from the Cam-CAN project (Shafto et al., 2014) that shows reliable stimulus-driven activity (i.e., significant inter-subject correlations) over nearly all cortical brain regions (Campbell et al., 2015; Geerligs and Campbell, 2018), we were able to study neural state segmentation across the entire cortex for the first time.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work describing the dataset.

claim: This study was able to study neural state segmentation across the entire cortex for the first time.
source: By using a large movie fMRI dataset from the Cam-CAN project (Shafto et al., 2014) that shows reliable stimulus-driven activity (i.e., significant inter-subject correlations) over nearly all cortical brain regions (Campbell et al., 2015; Geerligs and Campbell, 2018), we were able to study neural state segmentation across the entire cortex for the first time.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study.

claim: The median duration of neural states differed greatly between brain regions, ranging from 4.5 s in the voxels with shortest states up to 27.2 s in the voxels with the longest states.
source: The median duration of neural states differed greatly between brain regions, ranging from 4.5 s in the voxels with shortest states up to 27.2 s in the voxels with the longest states (see Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Most voxels showed median state durations between 5.1 and 18.5 s per state.
source: Most voxels showed median state durations between 5.1 and 18.5 s per state.
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the data.

claim: At the voxel level, there was a very high Pearson correlation (r = 0.85) between the median state durations of two independent groups of participants.
source: At the voxel level, there was a very high Pearson correlation between the median state durations of the two groups (r = 0.85; see Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The correlation between median state durations of two groups was lower at the searchlight level (r = 0.62) than at the voxel level.
source: This correlation was lower when we computed it at the level of searchlights (i.e., before projecting to the voxel level; r = 0.62).
evidence: This is a comparison of correlations from the data.

claim: Regional differences in neural state timescales are highly reliable across participant groups.
source: This suggests that regional differences in neural state timescales are highly reliable across participant groups and that the variability present in specific searchlights can be reduced substantially by averaging across overlapping searchlights.
evidence: This is an inference from the high correlation observed between groups.

claim: The variability present in specific searchlights can be reduced substantially by averaging across overlapping searchlights.
source: This suggests that regional differences in neural state timescales are highly reliable across participant groups and that the variability present in specific searchlights can be reduced substantially by averaging across overlapping searchlights.
evidence: This is an inference from the difference in correlations between searchlight and voxel levels.

claim: The timing of neural state boundaries was not associated with head motion.
source: The timing of neural state boundaries was not associated with head motion (see 'Supplementary results' in Appendix 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analyses in the supplementary materials.

claim: There were particularly short neural states in visual cortex, early auditory cortex, and somatosensory cortex.
source: Figure 1A shows that there were particularly short neural states in visual cortex, early auditory cortex, and somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: State transitions were less frequent in areas further up cortical hierarchy, such as the angular gyrus, areas in posterior middle/inferior temporal cortex, precuneus, the anterior temporal pole, and anterior insula.
source: State transitions were less frequent in areas further up cortical hierarchy, such as the angular gyrus, areas in posterior middle/inferior temporal cortex, precuneus, the anterior temporal pole, and anterior insula.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Particularly long-lasting states were observed in high-level regions such as the medial prefrontal gyrus and anterior portions of the lateral prefrontal cortex, particularly in the left hemisphere.
source: Particularly long-lasting states were observed in high-level regions such as the medial prefrontal gyrus and anterior portions of the lateral prefrontal cortex, particularly in the left hemisphere.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Very pronounced variability in state durations was found in the middle and superior temporal gyri and the anterior insula.
source: We found very pronounced variability in state durations in the middle and superior temporal gyri and the anterior insula, while the variability was consistently lower in all other cortical areas.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The variability in state durations was consistently lower in all cortical areas except the middle and superior temporal gyri and the anterior insula.
source: We found very pronounced variability in state durations in the middle and superior temporal gyri and the anterior insula, while the variability was consistently lower in all other cortical areas.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The variability in state durations was highly reliable across two independent groups of participants (r = 0.84 at voxel level; r = 0.54 at the searchlight level).
source: This effect was highly reliable across the two independent groups of participants (r = 0.84 at voxel level; r = 0.54 at the searchlight level).
evidence: This is a statistical measure of reliability from the data.

claim: In a nested cortical hierarchy, some boundaries at lower levels of the cortical hierarchy are thought to propagate to higher levels of the hierarchy until they are consciously experienced as event boundaries.
source: In a nested cortical hierarchy, some boundaries at lower levels of the cortical hierarchy are thought to propagate to higher levels of the hierarchy until they are consciously experienced as event boundaries.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on the nested hierarchy hypothesis.

claim: A large number of brain regions, throughout the cortical hierarchy, showed significant absolute boundary overlap between neural states and perceived event boundaries after FDR correction for multiple comparisons.
source: We found that a large number of brain regions, throughout the cortical hierarchy, showed significant absolute boundary overlap between neural states and perceived event boundaries after false discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons (see Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The anterior cingulate cortex, dorsal medial prefrontal cortex, left superior and middle frontal gyrus, and anterior insula show the strongest absolute overlap between neural state boundaries and perceived boundaries.
source: In particular, we observed that the anterior cingulate cortex, dorsal medial prefrontal cortex, left superior and middle frontal gyrus, and anterior insula show the strongest absolute overlap between neural state boundaries and perceived boundaries.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Neural state boundaries in the anterior cingulate cortex, dorsal medial prefrontal cortex, left superior and middle frontal gyrus, and anterior insula are most likely to underlie the experience of an event boundary.
source: This suggests that neural state boundaries in these regions are most likely to underlie the experience of an event boundary.
evidence: This is an inference from the overlap data.

claim: Regions across different levels of the cortical hierarchy (early and late) show a significant association between the neural state boundaries and perceived event boundaries.
source: This metric gives a different pattern of results, showing that regions across different levels of the cortical hierarchy (early and late) have strong overlap between neural states and perceived event boundaries (see Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Regions early in the cortical hierarchy, such as the medial visual cortex, the medial and superior temporal gyri, and the postcentral gyrus, show strong relative overlap between neural state and event boundaries.
source: Regions early in the cortical hierarchy, such as the medial visual cortex, the medial and superior temporal gyri, and the postcentral gyrus, show strong relative overlap.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Regions later in the hierarchy, including the anterior insula, most areas of the default mode network (DMN), and large parts of the lateral frontal cortex, show strong relative overlap between neural state and event boundaries.
source: The same is true for regions later in the hierarchy, including the anterior insula, most areas of the default mode network (DMN), including the medial frontal gyrus, anterior parts of the precuneus and the angular gyrus, and large parts of the lateral frontal cortex.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There is overlap between event and neural state boundaries throughout the cortical hierarchy.
source: These results suggest that there is overlap between event and neural state boundaries throughout the cortical hierarchy.
evidence: This is an inference from the relative overlap data.

claim: Boundary strength is defined as the Pearson correlation distance between the neural activity patterns of consecutive neural states.
source: Specifically, we define boundary strength as the Pearson correlation distance between the neural activity patterns of consecutive neural states.
evidence: This is a methodological definition.

claim: When neural state boundaries were weighted by strength, the absolute overlap with event boundaries increased compared to when binary definitions of neural state boundaries were used.
source: When we took the strength of neural state boundaries into account in this way, the absolute overlap with event boundaries increased compared to when we used a binary definition of neural state boundaries.
evidence: This is a description of the results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The increase in absolute overlap when weighting by boundary strength was observed particularly in the middle and superior temporal gyri, extending into the inferior frontal gyrus, as well as in the precuneus and medial prefrontal cortex.
source: This was observed particularly in the middle and superior temporal gyri, extending into the inferior frontal gyrus (see Figure 2C), but also in the precuneus and medial prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Boundaries that coincided with a larger shift in brain activity patterns were more often associated with an experienced event boundary.
source: This means that boundaries that coincided with a larger shift in brain activity patterns were more often associated with an experienced event boundary.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the boundary strength results.

claim: The overlap in neural state boundaries was significantly larger than chance for 85% of all pairs of searchlights.
source: We observed that the overlap was significantly larger than chance for 85% of all pairs of searchlights, suggesting that neural state boundaries are indeed shared across large parts of the cortical hierarchy (see Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Neural state boundaries are shared across large parts of the cortical hierarchy.
source: We observed that the overlap was significantly larger than chance for 85% of all pairs of searchlights, suggesting that neural state boundaries are indeed shared across large parts of the cortical hierarchy (see Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference from the overlap data.

claim: A perfectly nested architecture was not observed.
source: Although the overlap was highly significant for the majority of searchlight pairs, we did not observe a perfectly nested architecture.
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: The relative boundary overlap computed across two independent groups of participants was similar to the relative overlap computed within a participant group (r = 0.69).
source: We observed that the relative boundary overlap computed in this way was similar to the relative overlap computed within a participant group (r = 0.69; see Appendix 1—figure 6), suggesting that shared noise is not the cause of the observed regional overlap in neural state boundaries.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: Shared noise is not the cause of the observed regional overlap in neural state boundaries.
source: We observed that the relative boundary overlap computed in this way was similar to the relative overlap computed within a participant group (r = 0.69; see Appendix 1—figure 6), suggesting that shared noise is not the cause of the observed regional overlap in neural state boundaries.
evidence: This is an inference from the similarity of overlap measures across groups.

claim: State boundaries were shared within long-range networks.
source: We found that state boundaries were shared within long-range networks.
evidence: This is a description of the network analysis results.

claim: Some of the identified networks resembled canonical networks typically identified based on (resting state) time-series correlations.
source: Some of these networks resembled canonical networks typically identified based on (resting state) time-series correlations (see Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a comparison of the identified networks to known networks.

claim: An auditory network was identified that extended into regions involved in language processing in the left inferior frontal gyrus.
source: We identified an auditory network that extended into regions involved in language processing in the left inferior frontal gyrus, a fronto-parietal control network (FPCN), a cingulo-opercular network (CON), and a motor network.
evidence: This is a description of the identified networks.

claim: A fronto-parietal control network (FPCN) was identified.
source: We identified an auditory network that extended into regions involved in language processing in the left inferior frontal gyrus, a fronto-parietal control network (FPCN), a cingulo-opercular network (CON), and a motor network.
evidence: This is a description of the identified networks.

claim: A cingulo-opercular network (CON) was identified.
source: We identified an auditory network that extended into regions involved in language processing in the left inferior frontal gyrus, a fronto-parietal control network (FPCN), a cingulo-opercular network (CON), and a motor network.
evidence: This is a description of the identified networks.

claim: A motor network was identified.
source: We identified an auditory network that extended into regions involved in language processing in the left inferior frontal gyrus, a fronto-parietal control network (FPCN), a cingulo-opercular network (CON), and a motor network.
evidence: This is a description of the identified networks.

claim: The DMN was fractionated into anterior, superior, and posterior components.
source: The DMN we identified was fractionated into anterior, superior, and posterior components.
evidence: This is a description of the identified networks.

claim: The sensorimotor network (SMN) was split into a lateral and medial component.
source: The sensorimotor network (SMN) we identified was split into a lateral and medial component.
evidence: This is a description of the identified networks.

claim: A network overlapping with the dorsal attention network (DAN) was identified, although it only covered posterior parts of the DAN but not the frontal eye fields.
source: We also identified a network overlapping with the dorsal attention network (DAN), although the network we identified only covered posterior parts of the DAN but not the frontal eye fields.
evidence: This is a description of the identified networks.

claim: Two visual networks were observed, roughly corresponding to different levels of the visual hierarchy (early and late).
source: While the visual network is typically identified as a single network in functional connectivity studies, we observed two networks, roughly corresponding to different levels of the visual hierarchy (early and late).
evidence: This is a description of the identified networks.

claim: The networks with the longest state durations were the anterior DMN and the FPCN.
source: The networks with the longest state durations were the anterior DMN and the FPCN, while the early visual network, lateral SMN, and DAN had particularly short state durations.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The early visual network, lateral SMN, and DAN had particularly short state durations.
source: The networks with the longest state durations were the anterior DMN and the FPCN, while the early visual network, lateral SMN, and DAN had particularly short state durations.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A lot of variability in state duration was observed within networks, particularly in the auditory network.
source: Although regions within functional networks tended to operate on a similar temporal scale, we also observed a lot of variability in state duration within networks, particularly in the auditory network (see Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Many networks showed a clear within-network gradient of timescales, such as the auditory network, the SMNs, the posterior DMN, and the FPCN.
source: Many networks also showed a clear within-network gradient of timescales, such as the auditory network, the SMNs, the posterior DMN, and the FPCN (see Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The relative boundary overlap between regions is not simply driven by a similarity in the number of states, but rather by a similarity in the state boundary timings.
source: These results suggest that the relative boundary overlap between regions is not simply driven by a similarity in the number of states, but rather by a similarity in the state boundary timings.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of within-network gradients and the low correlation between overlap and state duration differences.

claim: The relative boundary overlap was highly distinct from the absolute pairwise differences in median state duration (r = −0.05).
source: This is also supported by the results in Appendix 1—figure 6, showing that the relative boundary overlap was highly distinct from the absolute pairwise differences in median state duration (r = −0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: The networks identified show overlap with functional networks previously identified in resting state, but they clearly diverged for some networks.
source: Although the networks we identified show overlap with functional networks previously identified in resting state, they clearly diverged for some networks (e.g., the visual network).
evidence: This is a comparison of the identified networks to known networks.

claim: The overall similarity with the previously identified networks by Power et al., 2011 was limited (adjusted mutual information [aMI] = 0.39).
source: This divergence was supported by the overall limited similarity with the previously identified networks by Power et al., 2011 (adjusted mutual information [aMI] = 0.39), as well as the differences between the correlation matrix that was computed based on the mean activity time courses in each searchlight and the relative boundary overlap between each pair of searchlights (Appendix 1—figure 6; r = 0.31).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison to prior network definitions.

claim: There were differences between the correlation matrix computed based on mean activity time courses and the relative boundary overlap between searchlights (r = 0.31).
source: This divergence was supported by the overall limited similarity with the previously identified networks by Power et al., 2011 (adjusted mutual information [aMI] = 0.39), as well as the differences between the correlation matrix that was computed based on the mean activity time courses in each searchlight and the relative boundary overlap between each pair of searchlights (Appendix 1—figure 6; r = 0.31).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: Regions with strongly negatively correlated mean activity time courses typically showed overlap that was similar to or larger than the overlap expected by chance.
source: Interestingly, regions with strongly negatively correlated mean activity time courses typically showed overlap that was similar to or larger than the overlap expected by chance.
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: The relative boundary overlap between each pair of searchlights was more similar to the absolute Pearson correlation coefficient between searchlights (r = 0.39) than when the sign of the correlation coefficient was preserved (r = 0.31).
source: Indeed, the relative boundary overlap between each pair of searchlights was more similar to the absolute Pearson correlation coefficient between searchlights (r = 0.39) than when the sign of the correlation coefficient was preserved (r = 0.31).
evidence: This is a comparison of correlations from the data.

claim: Pairs of regions that show negatively correlated BOLD activity still tend to show neural state boundaries at the same time.
source: This suggests that pairs of regions that show negatively correlated BOLD activity still tend to show neural state boundaries at the same time.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation data.

claim: The overlap in neural state boundaries was strongest for the searchlights that were part of the same functional networks.
source: It should be noted that although the overlap in neural state boundaries was strongest for the searchlights that were part of the same functional networks, we also found a lot of evidence for the hypothesis that boundaries are shared across different levels of the cortical hierarchy (see Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There is evidence that boundaries are shared across different levels of the cortical hierarchy.
source: It should be noted that although the overlap in neural state boundaries was strongest for the searchlights that were part of the same functional networks, we also found a lot of evidence for the hypothesis that boundaries are shared across different levels of the cortical hierarchy (see Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Overlap was particularly strong between all higher-order networks (DAN, CON, FPCN, and DMNs), as well as between the motor network and SMN.
source: Overlap was particularly strong between all higher-order networks (DAN, CON, FPCN, and DMNs), as well as between the motor network and SMN.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The sensorimotor, motor, and auditory networks showed highly significant overlap with the higher-order networks.
source: The sensorimotor, motor, and auditory networks also showed highly significant overlap with the higher-order networks.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Lower levels of overlap were observed between the early visual network and all other networks (except the DAN), as well as between the auditory and the sensorimotor networks.
source: Lower levels of overlap were observed between the early visual network and all other networks (except the DAN), as well as between the auditory and the sensorimotor networks.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The perception of an event boundary is more likely when multiple features of a stimulus change at the same time.
source: Previous research on event segmentation has shown that the perception of an event boundary is more likely when multiple features of a stimulus change at the same time (Clewett et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: When we took the within-network co-occurrence of neural state boundaries into account, the absolute overlap with event boundaries increased compared to when we used a binary definition of neural state boundaries.
source: We found that when we took the within-network co-occurrence of neural state boundaries into account in this way, the absolute overlap with event boundaries increased compared to when we used a binary definition of neural state boundaries.
evidence: This is a description of the results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When a particular neural state boundary is shared with more regions within the same network, it is more likely to coincide with an event boundary.
source: So when a particular neural state boundary is shared with more regions within the same network, it is more likely to coincide with an event boundary (see Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The effect of within-network co-occurrence on overlap with event boundaries was observed across all networks, except the early visual network.
source: This effect was observed across all networks, except the early visual network.
evidence: This is a description of the results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The effect of within-network co-occurrence was strongest for regions in the anterior DMN, the FPCN, and the auditory network.
source: It was strongest for regions in the anterior DMN, the FPCN, and the auditory network and slightly less pronounced for regions in the posterior and superior DMN, as well as the CON.
evidence: This is a description of the results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: On a regional level, the strongest effects of within-network co-occurrence were observed within the precuneus, angular gyrus, medial prefrontal cortex, temporal pole, insula, superior temporal gyrus, and the middle frontal gyrus.
source: On a regional level, the strongest effects were observed within the precuneus, angular gyrus, medial prefrontal cortex, temporal pole, insula, superior temporal gyrus, and the middle frontal gyrus.
evidence: This is a description of the results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Whole-brain co-occurrence showed stronger absolute overlap with event boundaries than within-network co-occurrence specifically for the early and late visual networks, the DAN, the lateral and medial SMN networks, and the motor network.
source: We investigated where absolute overlap for this whole-brain co-occurrence was stronger than when the neural state boundaries were weighted by within-network co-occurrence (see Figure 5B). This was the case specifically for the early and late visual networks, the DAN, the lateral and medial SMN networks, and the motor network.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For the auditory network, whole-brain co-occurrence showed lower absolute overlap with event boundaries than within-network co-occurrence.
source: For the auditory network, the opposite effect was observed; whole-brain co-occurrence showed lower absolute overlap with event boundaries than within-network co-occurrence.
evidence: This is a description of the results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: On a regional level, increases in overlap with event boundaries for whole-brain vs. within-network co-occurrence were most pronounced in the medial parts of the occipital lobe, the supplementary motor area and precentral gyri, as well as the superior parietal gyri.
source: On a regional level, increases in overlap with event boundaries were most pronounced in the medial parts of the occipital lobe, the supplementary motor area and precentral gyri, as well as the superior parietal gyri.
evidence: This is a description of the results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Boundary sharing had a positive impact on overlap with perceived boundaries, particularly for pairs of searchlights within the auditory network and between the auditory network and the anterior DMN.
source: We found that boundary sharing had a positive impact on overlap with perceived boundaries, particularly for pairs of searchlights within the auditory network and between the auditory network and the anterior DMN (see Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Neural state boundaries that were shared between the auditory network and the early and late visual networks, and the superior and posterior DMN were more likely to be associated with a perceived event boundary than non-shared boundaries.
source: In addition, we saw that neural state boundaries that were shared between the auditory network and the early and late visual networks, and the superior and posterior DMN were more likely to be associated with a perceived event boundary than non-shared boundaries.
evidence: This is a description of the results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Boundaries shared between the anterior DMN and the lateral and medial SMN network and the posterior DMN were more likely to be associated with a perceived event boundary than non-shared boundaries.
source: The same was true for boundaries shared between the anterior DMN and the lateral and medial SMN network and the posterior DMN.
evidence: This is a description of the results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Boundary sharing between the other higher-level networks (pDMN, sDMN, FPCN, and CON) as well as between these higher-level networks and the SMN networks was beneficial for overlap with event boundaries.
source: Boundary sharing between the other higher-level networks (pDMN, sDMN, FPCN, and CON) as well as between these higher-level networks and the SMN networks was also beneficial for overlap with event boundaries.
evidence: This is a description of the results shown in Figure 6.

claim: On a regional level, the strongest effects of boundary sharing were observed in the medial prefrontal cortex, medial occipital cortex, precuneus, middle and superior temporal gyrus, and insula.
source: On a regional level, the strongest effects of boundary sharing were observed in the medial prefrontal cortex, medial occipital cortex, precuneus, middle and superior temporal gyrus, and insula (see Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Four communities of timepoints were identified that vary in how their neural state boundaries are shared across the cortical hierarchy.
source: We used a weighted stochastic block model (WSBM) to identify groups of timepoints, which we will refer to as 'communities.' We found an optimal number of four communities (see Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Timepoints in the first community show the most widely spread neural state boundaries across the hierarchy, while timepoints in the later communities show less widespread state transitions.
source: These communities group together timepoints that vary in how the degree to their neural state boundaries are shared across the cortical hierarchy: timepoints in the first community show the most widely spread neural state boundaries across the hierarchy, while timepoints in the later communities show less widespread state transitions.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 7.

claim: From community 1–4, the prevalence of state boundaries decreased for all networks, but most strongly for the FPCN and CON, sDMN, aDMN, and auditory networks.
source: We found that from community 1–4, the prevalence of state boundaries decreased for all networks, but most strongly for the FPCN and CON, sDMN, aDMN, and auditory networks.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Boundaries that are observed widely across lower-level networks are more likely to traverse the cortical hierarchy.
source: This might suggest that boundaries that are observed widely across lower-level networks are more likely to traverse the cortical hierarchy.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the community analysis results.

claim: A similar drop in prevalence of event boundaries was found across communities.
source: We also found a similar drop in prevalence of event boundaries across communities, supporting our previous observation that the perception of event boundaries is associated with the sharing of neural state boundaries across large parts of the cortical hierarchy.
evidence: This is a description of the data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The perception of event boundaries is associated with the sharing of neural state boundaries across large parts of the cortical hierarchy.
source: We also found a similar drop in prevalence of event boundaries across communities, supporting our previous observation that the perception of event boundaries is associated with the sharing of neural state boundaries across large parts of the cortical hierarchy.
evidence: This is an inference supported by the community analysis results.

claim: Neural state boundaries throughout the entire hierarchy overlap with perceived event boundaries, but this overlap is particularly strong for transmodal regions such as the dorsal medial prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, left superior and middle frontal gyrus, and anterior insula.
source: In line with this hypothesis, we observed that neural state boundaries throughout the entire hierarchy overlap with perceived event boundaries, but this overlap is particularly strong for transmodal regions such as the dorsal medial prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, left superior and middle frontal gyrus, and anterior insula.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the study.

claim: The strong alignment in the anterior cingulate cortex suggests that the disparity between predicted and perceived sensory input may play a role in the experience of an event boundary.
source: In line with EST, the strong alignment in the anterior cingulate cortex suggests that the disparity between predicted and perceived sensory input may play a role in the experience of an event boundary (Holroyd and Coles, 2002; Kurby and Zacks, 2008), while the involvement of the dorsal medial prefrontal cortex is in line with previous studies linking this region to representations of specific events (Baldassano et al., 2018; Krueger et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations.

claim: The involvement of the dorsal medial prefrontal cortex is in line with previous studies linking this region to representations of specific events.
source: In line with EST, the strong alignment in the anterior cingulate cortex suggests that the disparity between predicted and perceived sensory input may play a role in the experience of an event boundary (Holroyd and Coles, 2002; Kurby and Zacks, 2008), while the involvement of the dorsal medial prefrontal cortex is in line with previous studies linking this region to representations of specific events (Baldassano et al., 2018; Krueger et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Some of the neural state boundaries that can be identified in early sensory regions are also consciously experienced as an event boundary.
source: This finding suggests that some of the neural state boundaries that can be identified in early sensory regions are also consciously experienced as an event boundary.
evidence: This is an inference from the relative overlap findings.

claim: Which of the boundaries in lower-level areas propagate to higher-order cortical areas may be moderated by attentional mechanisms.
source: Which of the boundaries in lower-level areas propagate to higher-order cortical areas may be moderated by attentional mechanisms, which are known to alter cortical information processing through long-range signals (Buschman and Miller, 2007; Gregoriou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: When participants are not attending the sensory input (i.e., during daydreaming), there may be much lower correspondence between neural state boundaries in higher- and lower-level regions.
source: When participants are not attending the sensory input (i.e., during daydreaming), there may be much lower correspondence between neural state boundaries in higher- and lower-level regions.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction.

claim: Neural activity around an artificially introduced event boundary can be effectively modeled by ongoing information integration, which is reset by a gating mechanism.
source: Recent work by Chien and Honey, 2020 has shown that neural activity around an artificially introduced event boundary can be effectively modeled by ongoing information integration, which is reset by a gating mechanism, very much in line with the mechanism proposed to underlie event segmentation (Kurby and Zacks, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neural states may represent information integration about a particular stable feature of the environment, which is reset when that feature undergoes a substantial change.
source: Similarly, neural states may represent information integration about a particular stable feature of the environment, which is reset when that feature undergoes a substantial change (Bromis et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Neural states in early visual cortex may represent short-lived visual features of the external environment.
source: This suggests that neural states in early visual cortex may represent short-lived visual features of the external environment, while states in anterior temporal cortex may contain high-level semantic representations related to the ongoing narrative (Clarke and Tyler, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: States in anterior temporal cortex may contain high-level semantic representations related to the ongoing narrative.
source: This suggests that neural states in early visual cortex may represent short-lived visual features of the external environment, while states in anterior temporal cortex may contain high-level semantic representations related to the ongoing narrative (Clarke and Tyler, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Neural state boundaries in transmodal cortical areas may not necessarily reflect one particular type of change.
source: Just as perceived event boundaries can be related to changes in one or multiple situational dimensions, such as changes in goals or locations (Clewett et al., 2019; Zacks et al., 2009), neural state boundaries in transmodal cortical areas may not necessarily reflect one particular type of change.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: State boundaries in transmodal regions are likely also dependent on the goals of the viewer.
source: State boundaries in these regions are likely also dependent on the goals of the viewer (Wen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Changes across multiple aspects of the narrative are more likely to result in an experienced event boundary.
source: It has previously been shown that changes across multiple aspects of the narrative are more likely to result in an experienced event boundary (Zacks et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Boundaries that were represented in more brain regions at the same time were more likely to be associated with the experience of an event boundary.
source: In line with this, we observed that boundaries that were represented in more brain regions at the same time were also more likely to be associated with the experience of an event boundary.
evidence: This is a summary of the co-occurrence findings.

claim: The strength of the neural state boundary can to some degree distinguish neural states that appear in subjective experience from the neural states that do not.
source: The strength of the neural state boundary, as measured by the amount of change in neural activity patterns, was also identified as a factor that can to some degree distinguish neural states that appear in subjective experience from the neural states that do not, particularly in temporal cortex, inferior frontal gyrus, precuneus, and medial prefrontal gyrus.
evidence: This is a summary of the boundary strength findings.

claim: A neural state boundary is not an all or none occurrence.
source: This suggests that a neural state boundary is not an all or none occurrence.
evidence: This is an inference from the boundary strength and co-occurrence findings.

claim: The reset of representations at neural state boundaries may differ based on what is happening in other brain regions, on the current attentional focus, or based on the degree of change in the representations of the environment in that particular brain region.
source: Instead, the reset of representations at neural state boundaries (Chien and Honey, 2020) may differ based on what is happening in other brain regions, on the current attentional focus, or based on the degree of change in the representations of the environment in that particular brain region.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Neural states in higher-level cortical regions represent an overarching representation that corresponds to many distinct states in lower-level cortical areas.
source: This sharing of boundaries across different cortical areas may suggest that neural states in higher-level cortical regions represent an overarching representation that corresponds to many distinct states in lower-level cortical areas, which all represent different features of that overarching representation (e.g., words spoken, characters on screen, or locations within a particular situation).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the boundary sharing findings.

claim: The sharing of boundaries across cortical areas is in line with previous conceptualizations of events as partonomic hierarchies.
source: This is in line with previous conceptualizations of events as partonomic hierarchies (Zacks et al., 2001a) and with other models of hierarchical neural representations, such as the hub-and-spokes model for semantic representations, which proposes that semantic knowledge is represented by the interaction between modality-specific brain regions and a transmodal semantic representational hub in the anterior temporal lobe (Lambon Ralph et al., 2010; Rogers et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The hub-and-spokes model proposes that semantic knowledge is represented by the interaction between modality-specific brain regions and a transmodal semantic representational hub in the anterior temporal lobe.
source: This is in line with previous conceptualizations of events as partonomic hierarchies (Zacks et al., 2001a) and with other models of hierarchical neural representations, such as the hub-and-spokes model for semantic representations, which proposes that semantic knowledge is represented by the interaction between modality-specific brain regions and a transmodal semantic representational hub in the anterior temporal lobe (Lambon Ralph et al., 2010; Rogers et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The sharing of boundaries is in line with a recently proposed hierarchical representation of episodic memories, in which items that are linked within small-scale events are in turn linked within large-scale episodic narratives.
source: It is also in line with a recently proposed hierarchical representation of episodic memories, in which items that are linked within small-scale events are in turn linked within large-scale episodic narratives (Andermane et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: This work provides the first cortex-wide mapping of timescales of information processing.
source: This work also provides the first cortex-wide mapping of timescales of information processing and shows that the DMN fractionates into faster and slower subnetworks.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study.

claim: The DMN fractionates into faster and slower subnetworks.
source: This work also provides the first cortex-wide mapping of timescales of information processing and shows that the DMN fractionates into faster and slower subnetworks.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings about DMN subnetworks.

claim: The validity of the results is supported by extensive validations using simulations.
source: The validity of our results is supported by extensive validations using simulations (see 'Supplementary methods' in Appendix 1 and Geerligs et al., 2021) and the reliability of our observations across independent groups of participants.
evidence: This claim refers to validation analyses in the supplementary materials and prior work.

claim: The validity of the results is supported by the reliability of observations across independent groups of participants.
source: The validity of our results is supported by extensive validations using simulations (see 'Supplementary methods' in Appendix 1 and Geerligs et al., 2021) and the reliability of our observations across independent groups of participants.
evidence: This claim is supported by the split-half reliability analyses.

claim: The validity of the results is supported by the similarity between the results and previous findings based on very different approaches.
source: It is also supported by the similarity between our results and previous findings based on very different approaches, such as experiments with movies and auditory narratives that have been scrambled at different timescales (Hasson et al., 2008; Honey et al., 2012; Lerner et al., 2011), or resting-state fluctuations in electrocorticography (Honey et al., 2012) and fMRI data (Stephens et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work using different methods.

claim: Neural states within a region were not of equal duration.
source: Although we characterized brain areas based on their median state length, we observed that neural states within a region were not of equal duration, suggesting that regional timescales may change dynamically based on the features of the stimulus.
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: Regional timescales may change dynamically based on the features of the stimulus.
source: Although we characterized brain areas based on their median state length, we observed that neural states within a region were not of equal duration, suggesting that regional timescales may change dynamically based on the features of the stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference from the variability in state durations.

claim: Event boundaries have previously been shown to align with changes in features of the narrative, such as characters, causes, goals, and spatial locations.
source: Event boundaries have previously been shown to align with changes in features of the narrative, such as characters, causes, goals, and spatial locations (Zacks et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The overlap between state boundaries and perceived event boundaries across the cortex suggests that characteristics of the sensory input are driving the occurrence of neural state boundaries.
source: Therefore, the overlap between state boundaries and perceived event boundaries across the cortex also suggests that characteristics of the sensory input are driving the occurrence of neural state boundaries.
evidence: This is an inference from the overlap findings.

claim: The timescale of information processing in particular brain regions is not only driven by stable differences in the rate of temporal integration of information, but also by the properties of the input that is received from the environment.
source: Together, these findings show that the timescale of information processing in particular brain regions is not only driven by stable differences in the rate of temporal integration of information, which may be associated with interregional interactions in the neural circuitry (Honey et al., 2012), but also by the properties of the input that is received from the environment.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings about variability and overlap.

claim: The medial prefrontal cortex and middle frontal gyrus have the longest timescales of information processing.
source: Our results show that some of the areas that were not covered in previous investigations (Baldassano et al., 2017; Hasson et al., 2008; Honey et al., 2012; Lerner et al., 2011; Stephens et al., 2013), such as the medial prefrontal cortex and middle frontal gyrus, have the longest timescales of information processing.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings about state durations.

claim: Regions at the top of the cortical hierarchy have the slowest timescales of information processing.
source: This suggests these regions at the top of the cortical hierarchy (Clarke and Tyler, 2015; Fuster, 2001) also have the slowest timescales of information processing, in line with expectations based on the hierarchical process memory framework (Hasson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the findings supported by citations.

claim: Neural state boundaries are shared across brain regions.
source: In line with previous work (Baldassano et al., 2017), we found that neural state boundaries are shared across brain regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the current data and a citation to prior work.

claim: Neural state boundaries are shared within distinct functional networks.
source: Our results show for the first time that these boundaries are shared within distinct functional networks.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current findings.

claim: Functional networks defined by state boundaries differ in their timescales of information processing.
source: Our results show that functional networks defined by state boundaries differ in their timescales of information processing.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings about network timescales.

claim: The posterior/fast DMN is particularly prominent in the precuneus and angular gyri, which are thought to engage in episodic memory retrieval through connectivity with the hippocampal formation.
source: The posterior/fast DMN is particularly prominent in the precuneus and angular gyri, which are thought to engage in episodic memory retrieval through connectivity with the hippocampal formation (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The posterior DMN has been proposed to be involved in forming mental scenes or situation models.
source: The posterior DMN has also been proposed to be involved in forming mental scenes or situation models (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Neural states in the posterior DMN may reflect the construction of mental scenes of the movie and/or retrieval of related episodic memories.
source: Thus, neural states in this subnetwork may reflect the construction of mental scenes of the movie and/or retrieval of related episodic memories.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on prior work.

claim: The superior DMN (or right dorsal lateral DMN) has been suggested to be a connector hub within the DMN, through which the FPCN exerts top-down control over the DMN.
source: This network has previously been suggested to be a connector hub within the DMN, through which the FPCN exerts top-down control over the DMN.
evidence: This claim refers to prior work about the superior DMN.

claim: The strong state boundary overlap between searchlights in the sDMN and the FPCN is in line with the sDMN being a connector hub.
source: This is in line with the strong state boundary overlap we observed between searchlights in the sDMN and the FPCN.
evidence: This is an inference from the overlap data.

claim: The anterior/slow DMN is particularly prominent in the medial prefrontal cortex that has been related to self-referential thought, affective processing, and integrating current information with prior knowledge.
source: The anterior/slow DMN is particularly prominent in the medial prefrontal cortex that has been related to self-referential thought, affective processing, and integrating current information with prior knowledge (Benoit et al., 2014; Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017; van Kesteren et al., 2012; Northoff et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Self-referential thought, affective processing, and integrating current information with prior knowledge require integration of information over longer timescales.
source: The current results suggest that these processes require integration of information over longer timescales.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding of long state durations in the anterior DMN.

claim: Event segmentation is often not considered in experimental settings, where events are predetermined by the trial or block structure.
source: Although event segmentation is thought to be a pivotal aspect of how information is processed in real life (Zacks et al., 2007), it is often not considered in experimental settings, where events are predetermined by the trial or block structure.
evidence: This is a statement about typical experimental practices.

claim: This study and previous work show that we are now able to investigate brain activity as it unfolds over time without asking participants to perform a task.
source: This study and previous work (Baldassano et al., 2017) show that we are now able to investigate brain activity as it unfolds over time without asking participants to perform a task.
evidence: This is a claim about methodological capabilities supported by the current work and a citation.

claim: The ability to investigate brain activity without tasks allows us to study brain function in a way that is much more similar to our daily life experience than typical cognitive neuroscience experiments.
source: This allows us to study brain function in a way that is much more similar to our daily life experience than typical cognitive neuroscience experiments (Hamilton and Huth, 2020; Lee et al., 2020; Willems et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: This opens the door for investigations of neural differences during narrative comprehension between groups of participants, such as participants with autism or Alzheimer's disease.
source: This opens the door for investigations of neural differences during narrative comprehension between groups of participants, such as participants with autism who may have trouble distinguishing events that require them to infer the state of mind of others (Baron-Cohen, 2000; Hasson et al., 2009), or participants with Alzheimer's disease, who may have trouble with segmenting and encoding events in memory (Zacks et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research possibilities supported by citations.

claim: This more naturalistic way of investigating brain activity comes at a cost of reduced experimental control.
source: It should be noted that this more naturalistic way of investigating brain activity comes at a cost of reduced experimental control (Willems et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about methodological trade-offs supported by a citation.

claim: Some of the differences in brain activity observed over time may be associated with eye movements.
source: For example, some of the differences in brain activity that we observe over time may be associated with eye movements.
evidence: This is a potential confound acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Preparation of eye movements may cause activity changes in the frontal-eye-fields.
source: Preparation of eye movements may cause activity changes in the frontal-eye-fields (Vernet et al., 2014), while execution of eye movements may alter the input in early sensory regions (Lu et al., 2016; Son et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Execution of eye movements may alter the input in early sensory regions.
source: Preparation of eye movements may cause activity changes in the frontal-eye-fields (Vernet et al., 2014), while execution of eye movements may alter the input in early sensory regions (Lu et al., 2016; Son et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In a related study, no age difference in eye movement synchrony was found while viewing the same movie, despite previous observation of reduced synchrony with age in several areas.
source: However, in a related study (Davis et al., 2021), we found no age difference in eye movement synchrony while viewing the same movie, despite our previous observation of reduced synchrony with age in several areas (particularly the hippocampus, medial PFC, and FPCN; Geerligs and Campbell, 2018), suggesting a disconnect between eye movements and neural activity in higher-order areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: There is a disconnect between eye movements and neural activity in higher-order areas.
source: However, in a related study (Davis et al., 2021), we found no age difference in eye movement synchrony while viewing the same movie, despite our previous observation of reduced synchrony with age in several areas (particularly the hippocampus, medial PFC, and FPCN; Geerligs and Campbell, 2018), suggesting a disconnect between eye movements and neural activity in higher-order areas.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited studies.

claim: Reducing the potential confound of eye movements by asking participants to fixate leads to an unnatural mode of information processing.
source: In addition, reducing this potential confound by asking participants to fixate leads to an unnatural mode of information processing, which could arguably bias the results in different ways by requiring participants to perform a double task (monitoring eye movements in addition to watching the movie).
evidence: This is a statement about methodological trade-offs.

claim: Event segmentation is underpinned by neural state boundaries that occur in a nested cortical hierarchy.
source: Here, we demonstrate that event segmentation is underpinned by neural state boundaries that occur in a nested cortical hierarchy.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The study included data from 265 adults (131 females) who were aged 18–50 (mean age 36.3, SD = 8.6) from the Cam-CAN project.
source: This study included data from 265 adults (131 females) who were aged 18–50 (mean age 36.3, SD = 8.6) from the healthy, population-derived cohort tested in stage II of the Cam-CAN project (Shafto et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: Participants were native English speakers, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing, and had no neurological disorders.
source: Participants were native English speakers, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing, and had no neurological disorders (Shafto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of participant inclusion criteria.

claim: Participants watched a black-and-white television drama by Alfred Hitchcock called Bang! You're Dead while they were scanned with fMRI.
source: Participants watched a black-and-white television drama by Alfred Hitchcock called Bang! You're Dead while they were scanned with fMRI.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The full 25 min episode was shortened to 8 min, preserving the narrative of the episode.
source: The full 25 min episode was shortened to 8 min, preserving the narrative of the episode (Shafto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the stimulus.

claim: This shortened version of the movie has been shown to elicit robust brain activity, synchronized across participants.
source: This shortened version of the movie has been shown to elicit robust brain activity, synchronized across participants (Campbell et al., 2015; Geerligs and Campbell, 2018).
